/api/taxonomy.rationale: The customer wanted to pay and the bank was the problem. Highest-value silent recovery there is — but only once the issuer is actually back. Retrying into a dead issuer converts at ~0% and pollutes our own success-rate signal for every other order on that bank.
Intent is real, balance is not. Time is the entire lever: the same account that declines on the 28th clears on the 2nd. Retrying in 5 minutes is theatre.

Best recovery bucket in Indian payments. The customer had their wallet out and lost the OTP race. A one-tap UPI intent link removes the exact step that failed, and it has to land while intent is still warm — minutes, not hours.
Expired card / bad CVV / dead VPA. The instrument is the problem, so a retry on it is a guaranteed decline. Needs a human to supply something new, which means one well-timed ask — not three.
Per-transaction or daily cap hit — UPI's ₹1L/day ceiling, or an international block. The rail is wrong, not the customer. Netbanking and EMI clear high-ticket where UPI structurally cannot.

Hard stop. A fraud/risk decline is a considered judgement by the issuer or our own risk engine, and hammering it is actively harmful: it raises our decline ratio with the network, trips velocity rules, and on some rails it is a compliance exposure. The correct recovery rate here is zero and the correct number of attempts is zero.

Our side or the gateway hiccuped — malformed downstream response, timeout mid-authorization. Cheapest possible recovery: retry quietly, customer never learns it happened. The one bucket where fast and silent is strictly correct.

They pressed cancel. That is a stated preference and we respect it: one soft, well-timed nudge, never an immediate one. Lowest recovery rate of any retryable bucket, so it also sorts last under a contact budget.

The classifier abstained. Abstention is a feature: guessing a bucket means guessing an action, and a wrong action on a live payment costs real money. Queue it, and let the miss rate drive the next taxonomy revision.
